intro.text:
Did you know that today's Trung Yên Alley was once linked to an ancient lake in Hanoi?

According to historical sources, this place preserves traces of the old Chung Yên village. The areas of Đinh Liệt and Gia Ngư once belonged to Thái Cực Lake, part of the network of waters around Hoàn Kiếm Lake. Over time, the lake was gradually filled in, and streets took shape.

Deeper inside the alley, you will come across Trung Yên Communal House, a monument with the tube-house architecture typical of the Old Quarter, ranked as a national monument in 2008.

Today, the smell of beef pho and fish noodles, and the calls of vendors taking orders, have become part of everyday life. Among the crowded eateries, Trung Yên Alley still keeps the story of a land that has changed across many generations.

nodes.name: Phở Sướng
nodes.summary: A long-running pho shop at the alley entrance, regarded by many regulars as one of the Old Quarter's recognized pho names.
nodes.story: At the Đinh Liệt end of Trung Yên Alley, an article about the alley notes Phở Sướng and its tái gầu beef pho. A separate report says the shop's name had been in use for about thirty years as of two thousand twenty-one, reflecting the owner's hope that diners would leave happy. That is a recollection reported in the press. We begin here without ranking the restaurant, then follow the alley inward.

nodes.name: Trung Yên Communal House
nodes.summary: A national-level architectural and artistic monument since 2008.
nodes.story: Farther inside, the route marks a stop as Trung Yên Communal House. The sources I could verify describe traces of old Chung Yên hamlet and the former Thái Cực Lake area, but I could not independently confirm details about the communal house itself. I therefore leave its date, worshipped figure, and heritage ranking unstated. We continue to the eateries documented in reports. That is where this story stops instead of turning an unknown into a fact.

nodes.name: Bún cá Sâm Cây Si
nodes.summary: A fish-noodle shop whose regulars playfully call it “bún cá sân si”; its specialty is fish wrapped around meat.
nodes.story: One report says bà Sâm once sold food beneath a banyan tree at Hàng Bè market; when the stall moved into Trung Yên Alley, the Sâm Cây Si name stayed. Another source mentions fish wrapped around meat and the playful name bún cá sân si. These are details recorded in the press; each visitor can form their own view of the food. The route places Bún ngan Nhàn next to this stop. The reports preserve different details, so I keep their accounts distinct.
nodes.caption: Bún cá Sâm Cây Si; its specialty is fish wrapped around meat with a crisp coating.

nodes.name: Bún ngan Nhàn
nodes.summary: A ngan noodle shop beside the fish-noodle shop, with a rich broth; at lunchtime, customers may queue for up to an hour.
nodes.story: The route places Bún ngan Nhàn beside the fish-noodle stop. One newspaper ranks it among Hanoi's best-known duck-noodle shops and reports that lunchtime visitors may sometimes wait more than an hour; the article also records mixed views of the service. Those are observations from one report, not a promise that the same thing happens every day. Experiences and wait times can vary. Next on this route is the chicken-pho stop.

An article about Trung Yên Alley mentions chicken pho in general, but does not connect it to Hương Trà. More about this particular shop needs an on-site check. alleyStory.title: Trung Yên Alley
paragraphs: Trung Yên Alley is about 200 meters long and preserves traces of the old Chung Yên hamlet. According to VietnamPlus (2024c), the land around present-day Đinh Liệt and Gia Ngư streets was once part of Thái Cực Lake, within the old network of waterways around Hoàn Kiếm Lake. From the late nineteenth century, the lake was gradually filled in and the area became dry land around the 1920s. The name Trung Yên is linked to the place name Chung Yên, but the timing and reasons for the change in spelling have not been clearly established in the available sources.

One notable historical remnant is Trung Yên Communal House at no. 10, also called Thanh Cẩm Temple. It honors a royal censor from the Mạc dynasty, has the tube-shaped architecture typical of the Old Quarter, and was recognized as a national monument of architectural and artistic value in 2008 (Hanoi Department of Culture and Sports, 2021).
Over roughly the past three decades, Trung Yên Alley has developed into a food destination with places such as Phở Sướng, Ngan Nhàn, and Bún cá Sâm Cây Si (VietnamPlus, 2024c).
Distinctive character: The alley brings together the history of an old village, a vanished waterscape, a place of worship, and today's food businesses.

eat.name: Phở Sướng
eat.dishes: Beef pho with a light broth; the shop is small and may be busy at meal times.
eat.hours: Reference hours: 05:30–12:00 and 17:00–21:30, depending on the day.

eat.name: Bún cá Sâm Cây Si
eat.dishes: Fish noodles, fish wrapped around meat, and fried fish cakes; the shop name is linked to Ms. Sâm and the banyan tree where she once sold food.

eat.name: Bún ngan Nhàn
eat.dishes: Ngan noodle soup, mixed ngan noodles, ngan, and mọc meatballs; the shop is well known, though reviews of its service vary.

eat.name: Phở gà Hương Trà
eat.dishes: Chicken pho in broth or mixed style, suited to breakfast.

visit.name: Trung Yên Communal House
notes: A national-level architectural and artistic monument since 2008.
Located on the second floor of a tube-house-style building and associated with worship of a royal censor from the Mạc dynasty.
The building has been restored; public visiting hours have not been confirmed (Hanoi Department of Culture and Sports, 2021; Vietnam National Authority of Tourism, 2023).

visit.name: Hàng Bè Market area and Gia Ngư Street
notes: You can combine a visit with observing local commerce, food shops, and everyday life in the Old Quarter.
The area can help illustrate the link between market life, trade, and the development of Trung Yên Alley (VietnamPlus, 2024c).
